finding.headline: Your taxes in retirement look low: about 10% of what you draw goes to tax.
details: Working, you pay no tax now because you have no pay. In retirement, you would draw about $39,906 a year and pay about $4,626 in tax, roughly 10%.

Most of your savings, about 81%, sits in a pre-tax account such as a 401(k). Withdrawals from it are taxed as income. Plan to take from taxable savings first, then the pre-tax account, and Roth money last.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Talk with a tax professional before you act, especially about when to start Social Security and how withdrawals affect your tax bill.

finding.headline: At 63, this household can claim Social Security now, but waiting longer raises the monthly benefit.
details: Social Security benefits can start as early as age 62, but full benefits come only at full retirement age. Delaying past full retirement age raises the benefit, and the increase stops at age 70.
Medicare coverage generally starts when you turn 65, and you are 2 years away from that age. Sign up for Medicare at 65 to avoid a possible late penalty.

finding.headline: The $64,000 yearly spending goal lasted in 0 of 100 market scenarios.
details: Basics were paid in 100 of 100 scenarios. The most you can spend and still be safe in 90 of 100 scenarios is $39,300 a year, about $3,275 a month, and that is $24,700 less than your goal.

The kept plan is a simple plan: stocks 15 points lower than the usual rule of age 110 minus your age, with Social Security claimed at age 70. Your savings were $590,000 at retirement and the median at age 92 was $0, so the money ran out in many scenarios.
Markets are uncertain, so these results are not promises. Spending nearer $39,300 a year, or more income or savings, would give more room.

finding.headline: You can count on $39,300 a year: $23,800 for basics and $15,500 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $23,800 a year.
Your spending goal of $64,000 a year lasts in 0 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $28,000 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70, which pays about $34,700 a year.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 92. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.

worth_checking.title: An income annuity
worth_checking.why: You are one person with savings that may not last in a long life. An income annuity trades part of your savings for a fixed sum each year for life. The sum loses value to inflation and the money cannot be taken back. This is information only. This is something to look into, not a recommendation. I have not priced it.
